title: Those who speak otherwise mean the same: a mere dispute about words
source_text: XXXVII. Sed qui aliter in hac materia loquuntur, non aliud tamen sentiunt. Nam impotentiam hominis circa bonum spirituale ideo moralem vocant, quia voluntaria est, & a vitio profecta: non quod putent in hoc genere hominem ex se posse quicquam facere vel conari, licet aegre, rarissime atque difficillime. Et ultro etiam concedunt talem impotentiam homini a primo ortu insitam esse, eamque propterea solum Physicam dici nolunt, quia non procedit ex carentia potentiae seu facultatis alicujus naturalis, sed tantum ex vitiosa & culpabili ejus corruptione: quod alii minime negant: adeoque hic est merum inter Reformatos de vocibus certamen.
pass_a_gloss: XXXVII. But those who speak otherwise in this matter, do not yet think otherwise. For they call man's inability about spiritual good moral for this reason, because it is voluntary, and proceeds from vice: not because they think that in this kind man of himself can do or attempt anything, though hardly, most rarely and most difficultly. And they also freely grant that such inability is implanted in man from his first birth, and they refuse to call it Physical for this reason only, because it does not proceed from the lack of any natural power or faculty, but only from its vicious and culpable corruption: which the others by no means deny: and so here there is a mere contest of words among the Reformed.
pass_b_english: Those who use different language here do not hold a different view. They call man's inability regarding spiritual good moral because it is voluntary and comes from vice, not because they think that man can do or even attempt anything of this kind by himself, however hard, rare and difficult the attempt.

They readily grant that this inability is ingrained in man from birth. Their only reason for not calling it physical is that it does not come from the lack of some natural power or faculty but solely from that faculty's vicious and blameworthy corruption, which the others do not deny at all. Among the Reformed, then, this is purely a quarrel over words.

lemmas.latin: merum inter Reformatos de vocibus certamen
lemmas.gloss: a mere contest of words among the Reformed

choices.why: Inability that lies in the will's settled disposition, opposed to physical inability (lack of the faculty or outside hindrance); kept as the technical pair.
